title: Two interfaces with the same default method

blocks.text: Java classes have one superclass, so the diamond problem cannot arise for state. Interfaces bring it back for **behaviour**: since Java 8 a class that inherits the same default method from two interfaces **must override it**, and the override may call either one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

items: `Duck.move()`: a duck is both, so it answers `"<Swimmer's move> and <Flyer's move>"`, built from the two defaults.

blocks.text: `Penguin` (a `Swimmer`) and `Bat` (a `Flyer`) are given, and neither overrides `move()`. Each interface's `name()` is implemented by the records.

new Duck("Donald").move()           -> "Donald swims and Donald flies"
new Penguin("Pingu").move()         -> "Pingu swims"
new Bat("Bruce").move()             -> "Bruce flies"

cases.says: A Duck, which inherits move() from both Swimmer and Flyer, combines the two defaults.
A Penguin, which only swims, gets Swimmer's default move() unchanged.
A Bat, which only flies, gets Flyer's default move() unchanged.

concepts: A class inheriting the same default method from two interfaces must override it, and may call one with InterfaceName.super.method().
A class extends one superclass but may implement several interfaces.
